learn.hook: The iron in your bicycle, the copper in your phone charger and the mica in your iron box all came out of India's ancient rocks.
points: India is fortunate to have fairly rich and varied mineral resources due to its varied geological structure; most valuable minerals are products of pre-Palaeozoic age, associated with the metamorphic and igneous rocks of Peninsular India.
A mineral is a natural substance of organic or inorganic origin with definite chemical and physical properties.

Characteristics: minerals are unevenly distributed over space; there is an inverse relationship between quality and quantity — good quality minerals are less in quantity than low quality ones; all minerals are exhaustible, take long to develop geologically and cannot be replenished immediately.
Minerals are the base of industrial development — iron for steel, bauxite for aluminium, coal and oil for energy.

topics.title: Distribution of minerals and the North-eastern Plateau belt

learn.hook: Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh sit on top of India's richest treasure chest of iron, coal and manganese.
points: Most metallic minerals in India occur in the old crystalline rocks of the Peninsular plateau.
Over 97 per cent of coal reserves occur in the valleys of the Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi and Godavari.
Petroleum reserves are in the sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High (offshore in the Arabian Sea); new reserves have been found in the Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins.
Minerals are concentrated in three broad belts, plus scattered occurrences: the North-eastern Plateau region, the South-western Plateau region and the North-western region.
North-eastern Plateau region: covers Chotanagpur (Jharkhand), the Odisha plateau, West Bengal and parts of Chhattisgarh; has a variety of minerals — iron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite and mica.

topics.title: South-western, North-western and Himalayan mineral belts

learn.hook: Rajasthan's marble built the Taj Mahal; Karnataka's Kolar gave India its gold; Kerala's beaches hide thorium-rich monazite.
points: South-western Plateau region: Karnataka, Goa and contiguous Tamil Nadu uplands and Kerala; rich in ferrous metals and bauxite; high-grade iron ore, manganese and limestone; Neyveli lignite (Tamil Nadu); monazite sands in Kerala; Kolar gold mines (Karnataka). It is less diversified than the North-eastern belt.

North-western region: along the Aravalis in Rajasthan and part of Gujarat; non-ferrous minerals like copper and zinc; building stones — sandstone, granite, marble; gypsum and Fuller's earth; dolomite and limestone for cement; Gujarat has petroleum; salt from Gujarat and Rajasthan.
Himalayan belt: copper, lead, zinc, cobalt and tungsten occur in the east and west; Assam valley has mineral oil deposits; oil is also found offshore near Mumbai (Mumbai High).

learn.hook: Bailadila means 'ox's hump': its hills in Chhattisgarh are shaped like one, and they hold some of the world's finest iron ore.
points: India has fairly abundant iron ore — the largest reserve in Asia; the two main types are haematite and magnetite, in great demand internationally because of superior quality.

Iron ore mines are close to coal fields in the north-eastern plateau region, which adds to their advantage. About 95% of reserves are in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.

Chhattisgarh: Dalli and Rajhara in Durg; Bailadila in Dantewada. Karnataka: Sandur-Hospet (Ballari), Baba Budan hills and Kudremukh (Chikkamagaluru). Maharashtra (Chandrapur, Bhandara, Ratnagiri), Telangana (Karimnagar, Warangal), Goa and Tamil Nadu (Salem, Nilgiris) also have deposits.

learn.hook: The copper in your house wiring may come from Khetri in Rajasthan, and the mica in old electrical insulation from the Gaya–Hazaribagh belt.
points: Copper is indispensable in the electrical industry for wires, electric motors, transformers and generators; it is alloyable, malleable and ductile, and is mixed with gold to give strength to jewellery.

Copper deposits mainly occur in Singhbhum district (Jharkhand), Balaghat district (Madhya Pradesh) and Jhunjhunu (Khetri) and Alwar districts (Rajasthan); minor producers: Agnigundala (Guntur, Andhra Pradesh), Chitradurga and Hassan (Karnataka), South Arcot (Tamil Nadu).
Mica is used mainly in electrical and electronic industries; it can be split into very thin sheets that are tough and flexible.

Mica areas: in Jharkhand, high-quality mica comes from a belt about 150 km long and 32 km wide from Gaya to Hazaribagh; Nellore (Andhra Pradesh) produces the best quality mica; in Rajasthan, a belt of about 320 km from Jaipur to Bhilwara and around Udaipur (with Ajmer and Beawar); also Karnataka (Mysuru, Hassan), Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and West Bengal.

Other non-metallic minerals include limestone, dolomite and phosphate (used in cement, steel flux and fertilisers). Map work: copper — Hazaribagh, Singhbhum, Khetri; bauxite — Katni, Bilaspur, Koraput; mica — Ajmer, Beawar, Nellore, Gaya, Hazaribagh.

learn.hook: Most of India's electricity is still generated by burning coal — much of it dug from Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
points: Mineral fuels are essential for generating power, needed by agriculture, industry, transport and other sectors.
Coal is mainly used in thermal power generation and in smelting of iron ore.

Coal in India occurs in rock sequences of two main geological ages: Gondwana (a little over 200 million years old), which holds most of the reserves, and Tertiary (about 55 million years old). About 80 per cent of Indian coal is bituminous and of non-coking grade.
The most important Gondwana coalfields are in the Damodar valley, in the Jharkhand–Bengal coal belt: Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih and Karanpura.
Jharia is the largest coalfield, followed by Raniganj.

learn.hook: Mumbai High, 160 km out in the Arabian Sea, was discovered in 1973 and changed India's oil story.
points: Crude petroleum consists of hydrocarbons in liquid and gaseous states, varying in chemical composition, colour and specific gravity; it occurs in sedimentary rocks of the Tertiary period.

It is essential for internal combustion engines in automobiles, railways and aircraft; its by-products feed petrochemical industries — fertilisers, synthetic rubber, synthetic fibre, medicines, vaseline, lubricants, wax, soap and cosmetics. Its value and many uses earn it the name 'liquid gold'.
Oil exploration became systematic after the Oil and Natural Gas Commission (ONGC) was set up in 1956; until then Digboi in Assam (where oil was struck in 1889) was the only oil-producing region.

Oil fields: Assam — Digboi, Naharkatiya, Moran; Gujarat — Ankaleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam, Kosamba, Lunej; Mumbai High (offshore, discovered 1973, production from 1976); Krishna–Godavari and Kaveri basins. Refineries are field-based (e.g. Digboi) or market-based (e.g. Barauni); map work: Mathura, Jamnagar, Barauni refineries.

Natural gas: the Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL) was set up in 1984 to transport and market natural gas; it is found with oil in all fields, with exclusive reserves along the east coast (Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh), Tripura, Rajasthan and offshore wells of Gujarat and Maharashtra.

learn.hook: Kerala's black beach sands hold some of the world's richest thorium deposits — fuel for India's future nuclear plans.
points: Uranium and thorium are the important minerals used to generate nuclear energy.

Uranium deposits occur in Dharwar rocks: along the Singhbhum copper belt (Jaduguda, Jharkhand); Udaipur, Alwar and Jhunjhunu (Rajasthan); Durg (Chhattisgarh); Bhandara (Maharashtra); and Kullu (Himachal Pradesh).

Thorium is obtained mainly from monazite and ilmenite in beach sands along the coasts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu; the world's richest monazite deposits occur in Palakkad and Kollam districts of Kerala, near Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) and in the Mahanadi delta (Odisha).
The Atomic Energy Commission was set up in 1948; real progress came after the Atomic Energy Institute at Trombay was set up in 1954, renamed the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in 1967.
Nuclear power projects: Tarapur (Maharashtra), Rawatbhata near Kota (Rajasthan), Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu), Narora (Uttar Pradesh), Kaiga (Karnataka) and Kakrapar (Gujarat).

steps: 1948 — Atomic Energy Commission.

learn.hook: Rajasthan's Bhadla solar park, one of the world's largest, sits where the sun shines almost every day of the year.
points: Fossil fuels are exhaustible and cause pollution; non-conventional sources — solar, wind, hydro-geothermal and biomass — are renewable, more equitably distributed and environment-friendly.

Solar energy is tapped by photovoltaic cells and solar thermal technology; solar thermal is cost-competitive, environment-friendly and easy to construct; used in heaters, crop dryers and cookers. Western India (Gujarat, Rajasthan) has great potential.

Wind energy is absolutely pollution-free and inexhaustible; turbines convert the kinetic energy of wind into electricity; permanent winds, monsoon winds, local winds and land and sea breezes can be used. Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka have favourable conditions.

Tidal and wave energy: ocean currents are a store-house of infinite energy; large tidal waves occur along the west coast (e.g. Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat), so India has great potential, not yet utilised. Geothermal energy: heat from the earth's interior, tapped via hot springs and geysers; a plant has been commissioned at Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh); Puga valley (Ladakh) also has potential.

Bio-energy: energy from biological products — agricultural residues, municipal, industrial and other wastes; it can give electricity, heat or cooking gas, improve the rural economy, reduce pollution and pressure on fuel wood. Example: the waste-to-energy project at Okhla, Delhi.

example.q: Suggest the best non-conventional source for: (a) Jaisalmer; (b) Gulf of Khambhat; (c) Manikaran; (d) a village with lots of cattle dung.
steps: (a) Sunny desert → solar.
(b) High tides → tidal energy.
(c) Hot springs → geothermal.
(d) Cattle dung and farm waste → bio-energy (biogas).

topics.title: Conservation of mineral and energy resources

learn.hook: An old aluminium can melted and remade uses about 95% less energy than making new aluminium from bauxite. Recycling is mining above ground!
points: Sustainable development requires integrating economic development with environmental concerns, conserving minerals and energy for future generations.
Alternative energy sources like solar, wind, wave and geothermal energy are inexhaustible and should be developed to replace exhaustible sources.

For metallic minerals, using scrap metals enables recycling — especially important for copper, lead and zinc, of which India's reserves are meagre. Using substitutes for scarce metals can also reduce consumption.
Export of strategic and scarce minerals must be reduced so that existing reserves last longer; improved mining techniques can reduce wastage.

Exam focus: classification of minerals; distribution of iron ore, manganese, bauxite, coal and petroleum; nuclear minerals; non-conventional energy; conservation measures; and map marking of mines and refineries.
